warmup.q: dish.stage is PLANNED. After val cooking = dish.also { it.copy(stage = Stage.COOKING) }, what is cooking.stage?
options: It doesn't compile: the block of also must return Unit
It throws, because data classes are immutable
warmup.why: also runs the block and then hands back the value it was called on. Its block has the type (T) -> Unit, so the copy the block makes is thrown away. Kotlin 2.4.21 compiles this without a warning. dish.let { it.copy(...) }, or simply dish.copy(...), gives you the copy.

opening:
Picture a good cook's small habits. You set up a new tray: paper on it, a little butter, twelve cookies, and the same tray goes into the oven. You note in passing, in the kitchen notebook, that tray two went in at ten past, and the tray goes in unchanged. You dip a spoon in the soup and get an answer back: needs salt. Each habit has one clear job, and from across the room you can tell which job it is.

Kotlin has five tiny functions for jobs like these: let, run, with, apply and also. Each runs a block of code with one value in hand. They look alike, and the compiler accepts almost any choice. Pick the wrong one and the code still compiles. It just hands back the wrong thing, quietly.

The last lesson's sequences passed each item on to the next step. These five pass one value into a block.

In this lesson, we'll write two of them by hand, pick one with two questions, run four bugs that compile without a warning, and treat null as a value. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a cook's small habits: set up a tray, note it in passing, taste with a spoon. Each became a scope function, picked by two questions, this or it and the value or the block's result. Then the picture broke: Kotlin doesn't hold a block to its habit's job, and the Elvis operator only looks at what's on its left.

Search your code for ?: run { and read the block just before it. Can it give null when the value it started from wasn't?

Next, we'll make failures into values. A null says nothing is here; how does a function say what went wrong?

sections.h: A scope function is a two-line function you could write yourself
sections.html:
Here's code from the recipe app that sets up a program for the oven and writes a line to the app's log, its running record of what it did. It's how most of us write it on day one:

Java
OvenProgram program = new OvenProgram();
program.setTemperatureC(180);
program.setMinutes(12);
program.setName("Oat cookies");
log.info("baking {}", program);
Kotlin
val program = OvenProgram()
program.temperatureC = 180
program.minutes = 12
program.name = "Oat cookies"
log.info("baking {}", program)

Nothing is wrong with it. It repeats program. on every line, and nothing marks where the setup ends. Kotlin code often says the same thing like this:

Java
// Java equivalent: a helper that takes a Consumer and returns the object
OvenProgram program = apply(new OvenProgram(), p -> {
    p.setTemperatureC(180);
    p.setMinutes(12);
    p.setName("Oat cookies");
});
log.info("baking {}", program);
Kotlin
val program = OvenProgram().apply {
    temperatureC = 180
    minutes = 12
    name = "Oat cookies"
}.also { log.info("baking {}", it) }

Those are the first two habits from the opening. apply sets up a new tray and hands back the same tray. also notes something in passing and lets the value go on unchanged.

apply and also look like keywords. They're ordinary functions in the standard library, a couple of lines each. Here are let and apply written by hand:

Java
static <T, R> R let(T value, Function<T, R> block) { return block.apply(value); }
static <T> T apply(T value, Consumer<T> block) { block.accept(value); return value; }
Kotlin
fun <T, R> T.myLet(block: (T) -> R): R = block(this)                 // value in as `it`, block's result out
fun <T> T.myApply(block: T.() -> Unit): T { block(); return this }   // value is `this` inside, value out

Both are extension functions: functions you can call on a value of any type T as if they were its own methods. The difference is the type of block. (T) -> R is a plain function type: the value arrives as the lambda's parameter, it. T.() -> Unit is a lambda with a receiver, which "Function types, lambdas and closures" showed briefly: inside the lambda the value is this, so minutes = 12 means this.minutes = 12. Java has no lambdas with a receiver, which is why the Java helper needs p. on every line.

The real let in the Kotlin 2.4.21 standard library is that same line plus two things:

@kotlin.internal.InlineOnly
public inline fun <T, R> T.let(block: (T) -> R): R {
    contract { callsInPlace(block, InvocationKind.EXACTLY_ONCE) }
    return block(this)
}

inline makes the compiler paste the block into your code, so no lambda object exists at run time ("Higher-order functions: functions in, functions out" explained why). The contract line is the next section's business.

So a scope function is one of these five small inline functions that run a block with one value in hand, the context object. They differ in exactly two ways: whether the block sees the value as this or as it, and whether the call hands back the value itself or the block's result. Two differences make a small grid, and two questions pick a cell.

try.title: One block, five functions, two answers
steps: Open ScopeReturns.kt. The same block, servings * 2, runs through all five scope functions. Write down what each line prints before you run it.
Run it.
On the also line, change also to let. Predict the output, then run it.
Read ScopeReturnsJava.java: what does Java write for each one?

code.title: ScopeReturns.kt
code.html: package workbench.functional.l06.demo data class Recipe(val name: String, val servings: Int, val grams: Int) class TraySetup { var paper: Boolean = false var cookies: Int = 0 override fun toString() = "TraySetup(paper=$paper, cookies=$cookies)" } // The two shapes, written by hand. A scope function is nothing more than this. fun <T, R> T.myLet(block: (T) -> R): R = block(this) // object as `it`, returns the block's result fun <T> T.myApply(block: T.() -> Unit): T { block(); return this } // object as `this`, returns the object fun main() { val recipe = Recipe("pancakes", 4, 200) // the same block, five ways: what comes back? println("let -> ${recipe.let { it.servings * 2 }}") println("run -> ${recipe.run { servings * 2 }}") println("with -> ${with(recipe) { servings * 2 }}") println("also -> ${recipe.also { it.servings * 2 }}") println("apply -> ${recipe.apply { servings * 2 }}") // the hand-written versions behave the same way println("myLet -> ${recipe.myLet { it.servings * 2 }}") println("myApply -> ${TraySetup().myApply { paper = true; cookies = 12 }}") }

alt.title: ScopeReturnsJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.functional.l06.demo; import java.util.function.Consumer; import java.util.function.Function; /** * Java has no scope functions and no lambdas with a receiver. This is what each one stands in for, * plus the two shapes written as static methods. */ public class ScopeReturnsJava { record Recipe(String name, int servings, int grams) {} static class TraySetup { boolean paper; int cookies; @Override public String toString() { return "TraySetup(paper=" + paper + ", cookies=" + cookies + ")"; } } // let: hand the value to a function, return what it returns static <T, R> R let(T value, Function<T, R> block) { return block.apply(value); } // apply/also: hand the value to a block, return the value itself static <T> T apply(T value, Consumer<T> block) { block.accept(value); return value; } public static void main(String[] args) { Recipe recipe = new Recipe("pancakes", 4, 200); // let, run and with all compute something from the object System.out.println("computed -> " + recipe.servings() * 2); // also and apply keep the object, whatever the block did System.out.println("kept -> " + recipe); System.out.println("let -> " + let(recipe, r -> r.servings() * 2)); // no receiver: the block must name its parameter and write t. on every line System.out.println("apply -> " + apply(new TraySetup(), t -> { t.paper = true; t.cookies = 12; })); } }

try.expect: let, run and with print 8, because they hand back the block's result. also and apply print Recipe(name=pancakes, servings=4, grams=200): they run the block and drop its result. myLet and myApply behave the same, because that's all the real ones do, and myApply prints TraySetup(paper=true, cookies=12). Changing also to let changes the value of the whole expression from the recipe to 8. In Java, "compute something" is a plain expression and "keep the object" needs a helper that takes a Consumer.

sections.h: Two questions pick the function: this or it, the value or the block's result
sections.html:
Because the five differ in only two ways, two questions pick one.

First, what should the call hand back? If you want the same value (to keep chaining it, return it or store it), use apply or also. If you want something new, a computed value or a different object, use let, run or with.

Second, how does the block use the value? If it mostly sets or calls the value's own members, a receiver (the value as this) reads best: apply, run, with. If it passes the value to other functions, or it also needs the this of the class around it, use an argument (the value as it): also, let.

The figure puts the answers in a grid. The Kotlin docs give the same advice as a list of purposes, and each purpose lands in one cell. Here they are with the kitchen habit that matches:

You want to Use In the kitchen In the recipe app
set up an object apply set up a new tray OvenProgram().apply { minutes = 12; name = title }
do something extra and keep the value also note it in passing menu.add(dish).also { log.info("added {}", it) }
run code on a non-null value, or compute from it let taste with a spoon guest.favorite?.let { recipes.find(it) }
use an object's members to compute a result run read the oven's own dials oven.run { preheat(); minutesLeft() }
run statements where an expression is needed run { } val grams = run { val base = recipe.grams(); base + extra }
group calls on a value you already hold with read off the card in your hand with(recipe) { "$name for $servings" }

run and with do the same job. with(x) { } reads well on a line of its own; x.run { } is the one that fits in a chain and after ?.. There's no ?.with.

The picture breaks in one place. A real kitchen habit can only do its own job: a note in the notebook can't change the soup. Kotlin doesn't hold a block to the job its function's name promises. An also block can change the object, and a run block can change it and return something else besides. The name tells the reader what you meant, and the compiler checks none of it.

The five share one more property, and it explains code that looks as if it shouldn't compile:

Java
// Java equivalent: a lambda can't assign a local at all, so this is a plain statement
Jar jar = fillJar(450);
final String label = jar.label();
Kotlin
val label: String
val jar = fillJar(450).also { label = it.label }   // compiles

A val may be assigned only once, and here the assignment sits inside a lambda. The compiler accepts it because also declares a contract, callsInPlace(block, InvocationKind.EXACTLY_ONCE): a promise to the compiler that the block runs right here, exactly one time. All five scope functions declare it. Write your own also without the contract and the same line fails with Captured values cannot be initialized because of possible reassignments. Contracts are an Experimental API that the compiler trusts and never checks; the Advanced Kotlin track covers them in "Contracts and context parameters".

Because the five are inline, a bare return inside the block returns from the function around it, not just from the block. In dish?.let { if (it.stage == SKIPPED) return; menu.add(it) }, a skipped dish leaves the whole function.

One caution before we go on. The pair x?.let { ... } ?: run { ... } looks like an if/else built from these pieces. It isn't always one, and the next section shows when both halves run.

code.title: ValInit.kt
code.html: package workbench.functional.l06.demo import kotlin.contracts.ExperimentalContracts import kotlin.contracts.InvocationKind import kotlin.contracts.contract data class Jar(val label: String, val grams: Int) /** Fills a jam jar and prints a label for it. */ fun fillJar(grams: Int) = Jar("J-${grams % 97}", grams) // a hand-written also: not inline, no contract fun <T> T.plainAlso(block: (T) -> Unit): T { block(this); return this } // the same plus what the stdlib adds: inline and an EXACTLY_ONCE contract @OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class) inline fun <T> T.contractAlso(block: (T) -> Unit): T { contract { callsInPlace(block, InvocationKind.EXACTLY_ONCE) } block(this) return this } fun main() { val label1: String val jar1 = fillJar(450).also { label1 = it.label } // the stdlib's also: compiles println("also: $label1 for ${jar1.grams} g") val label2: String val jar2 = fillJar(300).contractAlso { label2 = it.label } // yours, with the contract: compiles println("contractAlso: $label2 for ${jar2.grams} g") // Uncomment the next two lines and run again. The compiler can't know how often plainAlso calls the block. // val label3: String // fillJar(250).plainAlso { label3 = it.label } }

alt.title: ValInitJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.functional.l06.demo; import java.util.function.Consumer; /** Java equivalent: a Java lambda can't assign a local variable at all, so the assignment is a plain statement. */ public class ValInitJava { record Jar(String label, int grams) {} static Jar fillJar(int grams) { return new Jar("J-" + grams % 97, grams); } public static void main(String[] args) { final String label1; Jar jar1 = fillJar(450); label1 = jar1.label(); // a statement, outside any lambda System.out.println("statement: " + label1 + " for " + jar1.grams() + " g"); // Uncomment the next two lines and run again. javac rejects any assignment to a local inside a lambda. // String label3; // Consumer<Jar> keep = j -> label3 = j.label(); } }

try.expect: The first run prints also: J-62 for 450 g and contractAlso: J-9 for 300 g. With plainAlso, the build fails with Captured values cannot be initialized because of possible reassignments., because the compiler can't see how often the block runs. Without the contract, inline is not enough: the errors are 'val' cannot be reassigned. and Variable 'label2' must be initialized. The contract is what carries the promise. javac says local variables referenced from a lambda expression must be final or effectively final: Java never lets a lambda assign a local.

sections.h: Four bugs that compile without a warning
sections.html:
Scope functions are inlined, so they cost nothing while the program runs. Their cost is in reading. Each of these four compiles on Kotlin 2.4.21 without a warning, and each looks fine at a glance.

The first is ?.let { } ?: run { } used as if/else. Here it plans dinner. If a dish is open in the app, add it to the week's menu; if none is, download a suggestion and add that. menu.add returns the new slot id, or null when the dish is on the menu already:

Java
String planDish(Dish open, WeekMenu menu, Supplier<Dish> suggest) {
    return Optional.ofNullable(open).map(menu::add)   // map turns a null result into empty
            .orElseGet(() -> menu.add(suggest.get()));
}
Kotlin
fun planDish(open: Dish?, menu: WeekMenu, suggest: () -> Dish): String? =
    open?.let { menu.add(it) }          // add returns null for a dish on the menu already
        ?: run { menu.add(suggest()) }

It reads as "if a dish is open, add it, else download one and add that". But ?:, the Elvis operator, only looks at the value directly to its left: a ?: b gives a unless a is null, and then b. Here that value is the result of the let block, not open. The Elvis operator doesn't know or care where the null came from. So when the open dish is on the menu already, add returns null, and the planner downloads a suggestion and adds that too: both branches run. Java's Optional.map(...).orElseGet(...) has exactly the same trap.

?: tests the value on its left, not the value you started with. When the left side can be null, write if or when.

Or decide the value first: val dish = open ?: suggest(), then add it once.

The second is also or apply used to compute. dish.also { it.copy(stage = COOKING) } returns the original dish, because the block's type is (T) -> Unit and the copy is thrown away. dishes.apply { sumOf { it.servings } } returns the list, not the total. A declared type catches the second one: val total: Int = ... fails with Initializer type mismatch: expected 'Int', actual 'List<Dish>'. Nothing catches the first. When you want the block's result, use let or run.

The third is nested receivers. In tray.apply { timer.apply { minutes = 12 } }, the bare minutes binds to the innermost receiver that has one, timer. Delete minutes from Timer a year later and the same line still compiles, and now it sets tray.minutes. A change in one class has changed code in another. Java's double-brace initialization (an anonymous subclass with a block that sets fields) follows the same rule and has the same trap. Don't nest apply; name the target, as in timer.minutes = 12.

The fourth is a nested it. In cakes[id]?.let { tins[it.tinId]?.let { "${it.name}: ${it.sizeCm} cm tin" } }, the second it.name is the tin's name, not the cake's. Java can't make this mistake: it makes you name both lambda parameters and refuses to reuse a name. In Kotlin, name them, or better, flatten the chain:

Java
Cake cake = cakes.get(id);
if (cake == null) return id + ": no tin";
Tin tin = tins.get(cake.tinId());
if (tin == null) return id + ": no tin";
return cake.name() + ": " + tin.sizeCm() + " cm tin";
Kotlin
val cake = cakes[id] ?: return "$id: no tin"
val tin = tins[cake.tinId] ?: return "$id: no tin"
return "${cake.name}: ${tin.sizeCm} cm tin"

Each of the four hides behind a null or a nested block. Nulls, then, deserve a closer look.

code.title: ScopeBugs.kt
code.html: package workbench.functional.l06.demo enum class DishStage { PLANNED, COOKING } data class Plate(val id: String, val servings: Int, val stage: DishStage) class MiniMenu { private val onMenu = mutableSetOf<String>() /** Returns a slot id, or null when this dish is on the menu already. */ fun add(p: Plate): String? = if (onMenu.add(p.id)) "slot-${p.id}" else null } fun planOpen(open: Plate?, menu: MiniMenu, suggest: () -> Plate): String? = open?.let { menu.add(it) } ?: run { println(" no dish open, downloading a suggestion") menu.add(suggest()) } class Timer { var minutes: Int = 0 } class Tray { var minutes: Int = 0; val timer = Timer() } data class Cake(val name: String, val tinId: String) data class Tin(val name: String, val sizeCm: Int) fun main() { val soup = Plate("d1", 4, DishStage.PLANNED) println("1. ?.let { } ?: run { }") val menu = MiniMenu() println(" first plan: ${planOpen(soup, menu) { soup }}") println(" second plan: ${planOpen(soup, menu) { soup }}") println("2. also and apply drop the block's result") val cooking = soup.also { it.copy(stage = DishStage.COOKING) } println(" stage after also { copy }: ${cooking.stage}") val total = listOf(soup, soup).apply { sumOf { it.servings } } println(" total from apply { sumOf }: $total") println("3. nested apply") val tray = Tray().apply { timer.apply { minutes = 12 } } println(" tray.minutes = ${tray.minutes}, tray.timer.minutes = ${tray.timer.minutes}") println("4. nested it") val cakes = mapOf("k-1" to Cake("Lemon drizzle", "round-23")) val tins = mapOf("round-23" to Tin("springform", 23)) val label = cakes["k-1"]?.let { tins[it.tinId]?.let { "${it.name}: ${it.sizeCm} cm tin" } } println(" label: $label") }

alt.title: ScopeBugsJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.functional.l06.demo; import java.util.HashSet; import java.util.Map; import java.util.Optional; import java.util.Set; import java.util.function.Supplier; import java.util.stream.Stream; /** The same four bugs, as close as Java gets. Three of them exist in Java too; one Java's compiler prevents. */ public class ScopeBugsJava { enum Stage { PLANNED, COOKING } record Plate(String id, int servings, Stage stage) { Plate withStage(Stage s) { return new Plate(id, servings, s); } } static class MiniMenu { private final Set<String> onMenu = new HashSet<>(); /** Returns a slot id, or null when this dish is on the menu already. */ String add(Plate p) { return onMenu.add(p.id()) ? "slot-" + p.id() : null; } } static String planOpen(Plate open, MiniMenu menu, Supplier<Plate> suggest) { // Optional.map turns a null result into empty, so orElseGet runs: the same trap as ?.let ?: run return Optional.ofNullable(open).map(menu::add).orElseGet(() -> { System.out.println(" no dish open, downloading a suggestion"); return menu.add(suggest.get()); }); } static class Timer { int minutes; } static class Tray { int minutes; Timer timer = new Timer(); } record Cake(String name, String tinId) {} record Tin(String name, int sizeCm) {} public static void main(String[] args) { Plate soup = new Plate("d1", 4, Stage.PLANNED); System.out.println("1. Optional.map(...).orElseGet(...)"); MiniMenu menu = new MiniMenu(); System.out.println(" first plan: " + planOpen(soup, menu, () -> soup)); System.out.println(" second plan: " + planOpen(soup, menu, () -> soup)); System.out.println("2. peek drops the block's result, like also"); Plate cooking = Stream.of(soup).peek(p -> p.withStage(Stage.COOKING)).findFirst().orElseThrow(); System.out.println(" stage after peek { withStage }: " + cooking.stage()); System.out.println("3. double-brace initialization, Java's nested apply"); Tray tray = new Tray() {{ timer = new Timer() {{ minutes = 12; }}; }}; System.out.println(" tray.minutes = " + tray.minutes + ", tray.timer.minutes = " + tray.timer.minutes); System.out.println("4. Java makes you name both lambda parameters, and refuses to reuse a name"); Map<String, Cake> cakes = Map.of("k-1", new Cake("Lemon drizzle", "round-23")); Map<String, Tin> tins = Map.of("round-23", new Tin("springform", 23)); String label = Optional.ofNullable(cakes.get("k-1")) .flatMap(cake -> Optional.ofNullable(tins.get(cake.tinId())) .map(tin -> cake.name() + ": " + tin.sizeCm() + " cm tin")) .orElse(null); System.out.println(" label: " + label); } }

try.expect: The second plan prints no dish open, downloading a suggestion and then null, although a dish was open: the let block returned null, so run ran too. also { copy } leaves the stage PLANNED, and apply { sumOf } prints the list. The nested apply gives tray.minutes = 0, tray.timer.minutes = 12; after you delete Timer.minutes, the unchanged line sets tray.minutes = 12 and the compiler says nothing. The label is springform: 23 cm tin, the tin's name. Java shares the first three (orElseGet, peek, double-brace initialization) and gets the label right, Lemon drizzle: 23 cm tin, because both parameters have names.

sections.h: Nulls are values: ?., ?:, takeIf and requireNotNull
sections.html:
A Java developer new to Kotlin often reaches for Optional, Java's box that holds one value or nothing. You don't need it. A nullable type such as String?, a type whose values may be null, is not a box. In the words of the Kotlin docs, "at runtime, objects of nullable types and objects of non-nullable types are treated the same": the checks all happen at compile time. The operators do what Optional's methods do, with no extra object:

Java Optional Kotlin
opt.map(f) x?.let(f) or x?.f()
opt.orElse(d) x ?: d
opt.orElseGet(() -> ...) x ?: run { ... }, also lazy
opt.orElseThrow() x ?: throw ... or requireNotNull(x)
opt.filter(p) x?.takeIf(p)
opt.ifPresent(c) x?.let(c) or x?.also(c)

The right side of ?: can return or throw, because both are expressions in Kotlin. That turns a guard clause into one line, and every line after it works with a non-null value:

Java
String favorite = guest == null ? null : guest.favorite();
if (favorite == null) return "no favorite known: serve soup";
Kotlin
val favorite = guest?.favorite ?: return "no favorite known: serve soup"

takeIf { } is a filter for one value: the value if the test holds, null if not. It earns its place inside a chain, as in grams.takeIf { it > 0 }?.let(::weighOut). As a guard on its own, a plain if reads better. The test always runs, so keep side effects out of it. For collections, mapNotNull { } maps and drops the nulls in one pass.

When a null means somebody broke a rule, fail loudly and say why. requireNotNull(x) { "..." } throws IllegalArgumentException, for bad input from a caller. checkNotNull(x) { "..." } throws IllegalStateException, for our own broken state. Both carry a contract that tells the compiler x isn't null afterwards, so x is smart-cast from the next line on: the compiler treats it as the non-null type, because it can prove nothing changed in between. !! throws a NullPointerException with no message at all. Java's Objects.requireNonNull(x, "...") takes a message but still throws NullPointerException.

A null that means a broken rule should fail loudly. Use requireNotNull or checkNotNull, with a message, not !!.

Smart casts have one limit you'll hit. A var property is never smart-cast, because other code could change it between the check and the use. In the app's Scale class, if (lastReading != null) show(lastReading) fails with Smart cast to 'Int' is impossible, because 'lastReading' is a mutable property that could be mutated concurrently. This is where ?.let is the right tool: lastReading?.let(show) reads the property once. val reading = lastReading ?: return works too.

Arrow, the library in the next lesson, gives the same advice about its own Option type: "Typically, when working in Kotlin, you should prefer working with nullable types over Option as it is more idiomatic." It keeps Option for nested nullability in generic code and for libraries that don't allow null values.

That's the whole toolbox. The last section folds it into a checklist.

try.title: Four null tools, two languages
steps: Run NullTools.kt, then NullToolsJava.java. Compare the exception each null check throws.
In Scale.report, uncomment the if line and run. Read the error, then comment it out again.
Change the first line of starterFor to val favorite = requireNotNull(guest?.favorite) { "no favorite" }. Predict what happens to the second call in main. Is that better or worse here?

code.title: NullTools.kt
code.html: package workbench.functional.l06.demo data class Guest(val name: String, val favorite: String?) data class ShoppingLine(val item: String, val grams: Int?, val note: String?) class Scale { var lastReading: Int? = null fun report(show: (Int) -> Unit) { // Uncomment the next line and run: a var property is never smart-cast, even right after the check. // if (lastReading != null) show(lastReading) lastReading?.let(show) // reads the property once, then works with that value } } fun starterFor(guest: Guest?): String { val favorite = guest?.favorite ?: return "no favorite known: serve soup" // ?. chains, ?: can return return "start with ${favorite.lowercase()}" } fun main() { println(starterFor(Guest("Ana", "Tomato salad"))) println(starterFor(Guest("Ben", null))) println(starterFor(null)) // takeIf: a filter for one value; the result is nullable val grams = 250 println("takeIf positive: ${grams.takeIf { it > 0 }}, takeIf over 1,000: ${grams.takeIf { it > 1_000 }}") // requireNotNull and checkNotNull: a message, the right exception, and a smart cast afterwards val line = ShoppingLine("flour", null, "the strong kind") try { val g = requireNotNull(line.grams) { "shopping line ${line.item} has no amount" } println(g) } catch (e: IllegalArgumentException) { println("requireNotNull: ${e::class.simpleName}: ${e.message}") } val scaleUnit: String? = null try { checkNotNull(scaleUnit) { "scale not switched on" } } catch (e: IllegalStateException) { println("checkNotNull: ${e::class.simpleName}: ${e.message}") } // mapNotNull: transform and drop the nulls in one step val lines = listOf(line, ShoppingLine("sugar", 200, null), ShoppingLine("eggs", null, "free range")) println("notes: ${lines.mapNotNull { it.note }}") val scale = Scale().apply { lastReading = 450 } scale.report { println("the scale says $it g") } }

alt.title: NullToolsJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.functional.l06.demo; import java.util.List; import java.util.Objects; import java.util.Optional; /** The same null handling with Optional and Objects. Note which exception each check throws. */ public class NullToolsJava { record Guest(String name, String favorite) {} record ShoppingLine(String item, Integer grams, String note) {} static String starterFor(Guest guest) { Optional<String> favorite = Optional.ofNullable(guest).map(Guest::favorite); if (favorite.isEmpty()) return "no favorite known: serve soup"; return "start with " + favorite.get().toLowerCase(); } public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println(starterFor(new Guest("Ana", "Tomato salad"))); System.out.println(starterFor(new Guest("Ben", null))); System.out.println(starterFor(null)); // Optional.filter is the closest thing to takeIf int grams = 250; System.out.println("filter positive: " + Optional.of(grams).filter(g -> g > 0).orElse(null) + ", filter over 1,000: " + Optional.of(grams).filter(g -> g > 1_000).orElse(null)); // Objects.requireNonNull throws NullPointerException; Kotlin's requireNotNull throws IllegalArgumentException ShoppingLine line = new ShoppingLine("flour", null, "the strong kind"); try { Objects.requireNonNull(line.grams(), "shopping line " + line.item() + " has no amount"); } catch (NullPointerException e) { System.out.println("requireNonNull: " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + ": " + e.getMessage()); } // mapNotNull: map, then drop the nulls List<ShoppingLine> lines = List.of(line, new ShoppingLine("sugar", 200, null), new ShoppingLine("eggs", null, "free range")); System.out.println("notes: " + lines.stream().map(ShoppingLine::note).filter(Objects::nonNull).toList()); } }

try.expect: Kotlin prints IllegalArgumentException: shopping line flour has no amount and IllegalStateException: scale not switched on; Java's Objects.requireNonNull prints NullPointerException: shopping line flour has no amount. The if line fails with the smart-cast error, because lastReading is a var property. With requireNotNull, the second call stops main with IllegalArgumentException: no favorite. That's worse here: a guest without a favorite dish is an everyday case, not a bug, so the answer belongs in the return value. The next lesson makes that idea its whole topic.

sections.h: A checklist you can run in five seconds
sections.html:
When your fingers are about to type a scope function, run down this list and stop at the first line that settles it.

  1. Do you need one at all? A plain call, a?.b(), an if on a local val, or val x = y ?: return is often clearer. A scope function with one line inside is often a plain call in costume. Detekt, a tool that checks Kotlin code for style problems, ships UnnecessaryLet and UnnecessaryApply rules for exactly this case.
  2. What should the call hand back? The same value: apply or also. Something new: let, run or with.
  3. How does the block use the value? Its own members: apply, run, with. Passed to other functions, or the outer this must stay visible: also, let.
  4. Is the value nullable? Use ?.let, ?.run, ?.also or ?.apply, never with. If you add ?: something, make sure the block on the left can never produce null. If it can, write if or when.
  5. Is the block nested, longer than about five lines, or the third link in a chain? Extract a function or use named vals. The Kotlin docs ask you not to nest scope functions, because "it's easy to get confused about the current context object and value of this or it".

Try the list on one line: OvenProgram().apply { name = title }.also { log.info("baking {}", it) }. Line 1 has something to say about the apply: a block with a single assignment is exactly what detekt's UnnecessaryApply flags. Line 2 approves of the also: it's a side step, and the program flows on unchanged, like a note in the kitchen notebook.

compare.title: Set up, log and compute: scope functions vs plain Java

java.title: Bake.java
java.html: OvenProgram program = new OvenProgram(); // set up: a variable and setters program.setTemperatureC(bake.temperatureC()); program.setMinutes(bake.minutes()); program.setName(bake.recipe()); log.info("baking {}", program); // a side step is just a statement LocalTime doneAt = start.plusMinutes(program.getMinutes()); // compute String favorite = Optional.ofNullable(guest).map(Guest::favorite) // null check with a message .orElseThrow(() -> new IllegalArgumentException("no favorite"));

kotlin.title: Bake.kt
kotlin.html: val program = OvenProgram().apply { // set up: this, hands back the program temperatureC = bake.temperatureC minutes = bake.minutes name = bake.recipe }.also { log.info("baking {}", it) } // side step: it, hands back the program val doneAt = program.run { start.plusMinutes(minutes.toLong()) } // compute: this, hands back the time val favorite = requireNotNull(guest?.favorite) { "no favorite" } // null check with a message

compare.note: When the program runs, the two are the same. Every scope function is inlined, so the bytecode is the same local variable, setter calls and statements the Java version has. What differs is what the code tells the reader and what the compiler can check. apply puts the whole setup in one block, so the program is finished when the block ends, and also marks the log line as a side step that hands the value on unchanged. Java needs an Optional object to chain a null check; Kotlin's ?. and requireNotNull exist only at compile time, and requireNotNull smart-casts what follows. Java lambdas have no receiver and can't assign locals. That's why Java has no apply and no val inside also, and also why it can't have the nested-receiver bug.

steps.say: The app's "cook it again" button orders the ingredients of a recipe you've made before. shop.order returns null when the shop refuses the order. Here it is written as one expression. Before reading on, find every outcome that ends up in the wrong place.
steps.code: fun cookAgain(cmd: CookAgain): Outcome = recipes.find(cmd.recipeId)?.let { it.takeIf { it.cookedBefore }?.let { shop.order(it.ingredients, cmd.servings) }?.let { Outcome.Ordered(it) } } ?: run { Outcome.NotAvailable(cmd.recipeId) }

alt.html: Outcome cookAgain(CookAgain cmd) { return recipes.find(cmd.recipeId()) // Optional<Recipe> .filter(Recipe::cookedBefore) .map(r -> shop.order(r.ingredients(), cmd.servings())) // null when refused: map makes it empty .<Outcome>map(Outcome.Ordered::new) .orElseGet(() -> new Outcome.NotAvailable(cmd.recipeId())); }

steps.say: Three different failures come out as one. A recipe that doesn't exist, a recipe you've never cooked, and an order the shop refused all become null somewhere in the chain, so ?: run reports all three as NotAvailable. The app tells you the recipe is missing when the shop was only out of eggs. And there are four its with three meanings.

Rewrite it top to bottom. 1. Load, and leave early if it's missing. 2. Check the rule. 3. Do the work, and name its failure. 4. Put the happy path last. Each failure now has its own outcome, and no line depends on which it is in scope.
steps.code: fun cookAgain(cmd: CookAgain): Outcome { val recipe = recipes.find(cmd.recipeId) // 1. load ?: return Outcome.NotFound(cmd.recipeId) if (!recipe.cookedBefore) // 2. check the rule return Outcome.NeverCooked(recipe.id) val orderId = shop.order(recipe.ingredients, cmd.servings) // 3. act ?: return Outcome.Refused(recipe.id) return Outcome.Ordered(orderId) // 4. the happy path, last }

alt.html: Outcome cookAgain(CookAgain cmd) { Recipe recipe = recipes.find(cmd.recipeId()).orElse(null); // 1. load if (recipe == null) return new Outcome.NotFound(cmd.recipeId()); if (!recipe.cookedBefore()) // 2. check the rule return new Outcome.NeverCooked(recipe.id()); String orderId = shop.order(recipe.ingredients(), cmd.servings()); // 3. act if (orderId == null) return new Outcome.Refused(recipe.id()); return new Outcome.Ordered(orderId); // 4. the happy path, last }

steps.say: A scope function still has a place here: a side step that must not change the result. also logs the outcome and hands it on unchanged, which is what the reader expects from the word.
steps.code: return Outcome.Ordered(orderId) .also { log.info("cook again: {}", it) } // side step: the value flows through

alt.html: Outcome outcome = new Outcome.Ordered(orderId); log.info("cook again: {}", outcome); // Java: just a statement return outcome;

lab.title: Fix four scope-function bugs in the meal planner
steps: Run the tests. Four of ten fail, one for each function in Planner.kt. Read each failure message before you read the code. Model.kt holds the types and needs no changes.
planDish: an open dish that is on the menu already must not trigger a download or a second add. Rewrite it without ?: run.
startCooking: return the copy marked COOKING.
ovenProgram: the recipe's name belongs on program.name, the oven's screen, not on program.timer.name.
tinLabel: show the cake's name, not the tin's. Use named values instead of it.
Run the tests until all ten pass. Then run the five-second checklist over your four functions.
hints: For planDish, decide the dish first (open ?: suggest()), then add it once. ?: return handles the dish that is on the menu already.
startCooking is a two-branch if expression. It needs no scope function.
In ovenProgram, a nested apply with one line inside can become timer.beep = "long".
In tinLabel, two vals, each with ?: return "...", read top to bottom and can't mix up the cake and the tin.

drill.title: The grid from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Draw the 2x2 grid (this or it, the value or the block's result) and put the five functions in it, with the kitchen habit for each. Then write one recipe-app line for each function, and next to it, what the whole expression gives back. Check your grid against the figure.

answer.html: // hands back the value | hands back the block's result // this: apply (set up a new tray) | run, with (read the dials) // it: also (note in passing) | let (taste with a spoon) val program = OvenProgram().apply { minutes = 12; name = "Oat cookies" } // the program val slot = menu.add(dish).also { log.info("added {}", it) } // the slot id, or null val doneAt = program.run { start.plusMinutes(minutes.toLong()) } // the time val line = with(recipe) { "$name for $servings" } // the String val found = guest.favorite?.let { recipes.find(it) } // the search result, or null

alt.html: // Java has no scope functions; each line is the plain Java it stands for OvenProgram program = new OvenProgram(); program.setMinutes(12); program.setName("Oat cookies"); String slot = menu.add(dish); log.info("added {}", slot); LocalTime doneAt = start.plusMinutes(program.getMinutes()); String line = recipe.name() + " for " + recipe.servings(); Recipe found = guest.favorite() == null ? null : recipes.find(guest.favorite());

recap: A scope function is a tiny inline function: it runs a block with the value as this (run, with, apply) or it (let, also), and hands back the value (apply, also) or the block's result (let, run, with).
Pick by two questions: what should the call hand back, and does the block use the value's members or pass the value along?
All five are inline and declare callsInPlace(block, EXACTLY_ONCE): no lambda objects, a val can be assigned inside, and a bare return leaves the enclosing function.
x?.let { A } ?: B runs B whenever A gives null, not only when x is null. When A can be null, write if or when.
Nullable types replace Optional: ?. maps, ?: defaults, returns or throws, takeIf filters, and requireNotNull/checkNotNull fail with a message and smart-cast.
The limit: a scope function's name only states your intent. The compiler checks types, not jobs, so also { copy() }, nested receivers and nested it all compile without a warning.

explain.prompt: A teammate writes recipes.find(id)?.let { cache.put(id, it) } ?: run { log.warn("missing $id") } and says it means "cache it if found, warn if not". cache is a HashMap. Explain when it does something else, and what you'd write instead.
explain.answer: The Elvis operator doesn't look at what find returned. It looks at the value of the whole left side, which is the result of the let block, and that is whatever cache.put returned. HashMap.put returns the previous value for the key, which is null the first time. So every time a recipe is found and cached for the first time, the block gives null and the warning runs too: "missing" gets logged for recipes that were found. It only behaves as intended when an older value was already cached. I'd write the branch I mean: val recipe = recipes.find(id); if (recipe != null) cache[id] = recipe else log.warn("missing $id"). Or, since caching is only a side step, recipes.find(id)?.also { cache[id] = it } ?: log.warn(...), because also hands back the recipe itself, which is not null.

deeper.html:
Two things are changing around scope functions, and one tool can enforce the checklist for you.

The return-value checker. Kotlin 2.3.0 added an Experimental checker that warns when you ignore a function's result. It's off by default; -Xreturn-value-checker=check reports ignored results of functions the standard library marks, and full treats every function as marked. In Kotlin 2.4.21, all six scope functions (the five plus non-extension run) carry @IgnorableReturnValue, so dish.let { it.copy(stage = COOKING) } as a bare statement is not reported. takeIf and takeUnless don't carry it. On the standard library's main branch, after 2.4.21, let, run and with have dropped @IgnorableReturnValue for a new returnsResultOf(block) contract, which Kotlin 2.4.0 introduced as Experimental. With it, the checker can tell x?.let { builder.append(it) } (fine to ignore) from x?.let { "kotlin.$it" } (a value you computed and dropped). Which release will ship that change isn't known yet. apply and also keep @IgnorableReturnValue, so the also { it.copy() } bug stays invisible to the checker.

Labels for nested receivers. When you can't avoid a nested receiver, this@label says which one you mean. Two nested apply blocks share the implicit label @apply, so you need your own: tray.apply outer@{ timer.apply { this@outer.minutes = 12 } }. If you need a label, that's usually a sign to flatten the code instead.

Detekt. Detekt 1.23.8, the current stable release, has rules for most of the checklist: UnnecessaryLet, UnnecessaryApply (active by default since 1.16.0), AlsoCouldBeApply and UseLet in the style rule set, and NestedScopeFunctions in the complexity rule set. Apart from UnnecessaryApply, they're off until you enable them. UseLet pulls the other way from UnnecessaryLet: it wants if (x != null) f(x) else null written as x?.let { f(it) }. A rule of thumb that satisfies both: use ?.let when the non-null value flows into an expression, and use if on a local val for control flow and for branches with more than one statement.
